clue.text: Time sorted out a crisis related to old age

parts.note: T is the standard abbreviation for time

indicators.note: to sort something out is to put it into a new order, so these letters get rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone finally dealt with a crisis that came with getting old.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old age' looks like a person's later years, but here an age is a geological period. T comes first, then the shuffled letters of 'a crisis'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Triassic is an ancient geological period, so the adjective describes things belonging to that very old age of Earth's history.

clue.text: Hot and steamy pair messing around with clot

indicators.note: messing around with something puts it out of its proper order, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sultry couple fooling about with a dimwit, which reads like a racy tabloid story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot and steamy' suggests romance, and a clot is a fool, but both words after the indicator are just letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Tropical climates are characteristically humid and warm, so the adjective fits weather that is both sweltering and muggy.

clue.text: I, at the office, help with the turnover

parts.note: someone at the office is in, at work

indicators.note: turning something over flips it end to end, so this piece is read backwards

parts.note: aid is help

explanation.surface: A worker announces that they assist with the company's annual turnover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I' looks like the speaker but is the definition: INDIA is the word for the letter I in the NATO phonetic alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: In the radio spelling alphabet used by pilots and soldiers, the letter I is spoken as this country's name.

clue.text: Star involved with East German officer

indicators.note: something involved is tangled and convoluted, so these letters are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A celebrity has been caught up with a Cold War-era official from the GDR.
explanation.walkthrough: All fourteen letters of 'Star' and 'East German' are rearranged; 'officer' could easily be read as part of the German character.
explanation.definitionFit: A serjeant at arms is an official who keeps order in a legislature or court, an officer of that body.

clue.text: Cold dessert and hot served up for old folk

parts.note: an ice is a frozen dessert

indicators.note: in a down clue, being sent upwards means reading from the bottom, so the order flips

parts.note: hot in the sense of fashionable, in

explanation.surface: Ice cream and a hot pudding are served to elderly residents of a care home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old folk' suggests pensioners, but it means an ancient people. The Iceni were the tribe of Boudicca in East Anglia during Roman Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: The Iceni were an ancient British tribe, a people of long ago, so they are literally folk from old times.

clue.text: You have to say god is lazy

indicators.note: this word is only correct when spoken, since you must utter it for the sound to count

parts.note: an idol is a god that is worshipped

explanation.surface: Someone insists that a deity is a layabout.
explanation.walkthrough: An idol, an image worshipped as a god, is pronounced exactly like the word meaning lazy.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe someone avoiding work and doing nothing at all, inactive and slothful.

clue.text: On the way home, model-type executed pose

parts.note: someone at home is in
the Model T was Ford's famous car, so this type of model is T
to run a plan is to execute it
to sit for an artist is to pose

explanation.surface: A fashion model, heading home, struck a pose that was carried out perfectly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the way home' looks like a single phrase, but the definition stops at 'way'; 'home' starts the wordplay. 'Executed' means carried out, not killed.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods or travellers that are en route, being carried between places, are said to be in transit.

clue.text: One who really desires more of a Marathon?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a person who longs, yearns
second meaning: comparative of long, as a marathon is long

explanation.walkthrough: The first reading is a noun formed from the verb meaning yearn; the second is the comparative adjective, with a marathon standing for anything long.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who yearns is one who longs, and something stretching further than a lengthy race is of greater length.

clue.text: More illicit pay arranged for MP

indicators.note: arranging things sets them out in an order of your choosing, so the letters are reordered

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Extra under-the-counter cash has been fixed up for a Member of Parliament.
explanation.walkthrough: MP looks like a Member of Parliament, which fits a bribery story, but here it stands for the army's own law enforcers.
explanation.definitionFit: MP is the standard abbreviation for the corps that polices soldiers, as well as for a single member of it.

clue.text: Fighter by senior designer of the A5 plane?

parts.note: F designates a fighter aircraft, as in the F-16
a senior is older

explanation.surface: A warplane next to an elder engineer who created some new aircraft model.
explanation.walkthrough: A5 sounds like an aircraft type, but it is a paper size: fold a sheet of A4 in half and you get A5, so a paper plane comes from someone who folds.
explanation.definitionFit: A paper aeroplane is made by creasing paper, so its maker is one who folds, playfully called its designer.

clue.text: Being old is no good, receding relations admitted

parts.note: ex- means former, so an ex is someone or something old

indicators.note: to be admitted is to be let in, so the turned word goes inside the other letters
something receding goes backwards, so the word is read in reverse

parts.note: it is a coy word for sex, sexual relations

explanation.surface: A gloomy verdict that growing old is no good once family ties start fading away.
explanation.walkthrough: Relations here are sexual ones, coyly called 'it'. 'Being' looks like a verb, but the definition is the adjective for something that is.
explanation.definitionFit: Existing and being both describe what currently is or is in existence, as in the existing system or the system now being.

clue.text: Easterly wind going over grand foreign capital

indicators.note: in an across clue, heading east to west means reading from right to left
something going over another covers it on both sides, so it wraps around

parts.note: air is moving wind
G is the abbreviation for grand, a thousand

explanation.surface: A wind from the east blows across a magnificent city abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: An easterly wind blows from the east towards the west, which in an across clue is right to left. AIR wraps G, and the whole is then read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Riga is the capital city of Latvia, so to a British setter it is a capital in another country.

clue.text: Long Island iced tea and lime in New Delhi's top

definitions.note: iced is American slang for killed, and Long Island here marks it as a New York usage

indicators.note: new means made afresh, so the letters are made into a fresh arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: the top of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the word whose first letter is taken

explanation.surface: A Long Island iced tea, the strong cocktail, mixed with lime in New Delhi.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long Island iced tea' looks like one cocktail, but the definition stops at 'iced', gangster slang for killed, with 'Long Island' flagging it as American. 'New' rearranges TEA, LIME and IN, and 'top' adds the D of Delhi.
explanation.definitionFit: To ice someone is American underworld slang for to murder them, and eliminated is the same euphemism for killed.

clue.text: Is a giant slob in need of styling clippers?

indicators.note: styling restyles and reshapes, so the letters need a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A huge scruffy man needs a haircut, so should he reach for the hair clippers?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clippers' and 'styling' point to a barber, but clippers are also fast sailing ships of the nineteenth century.
explanation.definitionFit: Clippers were fast, sleek merchant vessels driven by canvas, so they are examples of wind-powered ships.

clue.text: Aussie holiday or party time …

parts.note: Labour is a political party in both Britain and Australia
a day is a period of time

explanation.surface: An Australian deciding between a public holiday and a party.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs the sentence on into the next clue, but each clue is solved on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Australian states each celebrate a public holiday honouring workers and the eight-hour working movement under this name.

clue.text: … in which one might plonk plonk?

definitions.text: … in which one might plonk plonk?

parts.words: … in which one might plonk plonk?
parts.note: surface reading: a place to dump something down carelessly at a party; setter's reading: the second plonk is cheap wine, stored in a rack or receptacle for wine bottles

explanation.walkthrough: Plonk is British slang for cheap wine, and to plonk is to set something down heavily. A wine bin is a storage rack, and any bin is somewhere to plonk things.
explanation.definitionFit: A wine cellar stores bottles in compartments called bins, and a rubbish container is a place to drop unwanted bottles.

clue.text: Cutting down drinking a little around noon

indicators.note: to be around something is to surround it, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: to sip is to drink a small amount
N is the abbreviation for noon

explanation.surface: Someone is cutting back on alcohol, having just a little around midday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cutting down' reads as reducing drinking, but it is the definition, meaning trimming with scissors.
explanation.definitionFit: Snipping is cutting with small, quick strokes of scissors, which trims something down in size.

clue.text: One some bend over backwards for and then smack?

definitions.text: One some bend over backwards for and then smack?

parts.words: One some bend over backwards for and then smack?
parts.note: surface reading: someone people make huge efforts for, then strike in anger; setter's reading: visitors to an Irish castle lean back literally, then plant a kiss, smack being a loud kiss

explanation.walkthrough: To bend over backwards is an idiom for trying hard, but here it is literal: at Blarney Castle in Ireland, visitors lean back over a drop to kiss a famous rock said to grant eloquence. A smack is a kiss.
explanation.definitionFit: Tourists at the County Cork castle are held as they lean backwards to kiss this rock, which legend says bestows the gift of the gab.

clue.text: Join the Tory party — it's a shining light

parts.note: to join a group is to become part of it, so you will be
a Tory is a Conservative, abbreviated Con, so joining makes one a member

explanation.surface: A political recruiting slogan: sign up with the Conservatives, they are a guiding light.
explanation.walkthrough: Joining the Tories means you would be a Con, since Con is the usual abbreviation for a Conservative; read as one word it becomes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A beacon is a signal fire or lamp, and figuratively a shining light is an inspiring example, as a beacon of hope.

clue.text: Outfit with German officer at the front in push

parts.note: a get-up is an outfit, a costume
with means and, together
G is the abbreviation for German

indicators.note: the front of a word is where it begins, so only its first letter is used

parts.note: the opening letter of this word

explanation.surface: A uniform worn by a German commander leading an advance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'German officer' reads as one person, but they split: G for German, then only the first letter of 'officer'. 'Push' is a noun meaning drive.
explanation.definitionFit: Push in the sense of drive, energy and ambition is what someone with enthusiasm and initiative has.

clue.text: A hard villain brought about Russian retreat

indicators.note: to bring a ship about is to turn it to face the other way, so the order turns round

parts.note: taken as written
H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard
a cad is a dishonourable man, a rogue

explanation.surface: A tough villain caused the Russian army to fall back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retreat' reads as a military withdrawal, but it is a noun for a hideaway, and 'brought about' looks like caused rather than turned around.
explanation.definitionFit: A dacha is a Russian country cottage used as a holiday home, a place to get away from the city.

clue.text: Range of beers European exported for head of Pilsner

indicators.note: the letter for European is sent out of the word and replaced by the new one

parts.note: ales are beers

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the word whose first letter is taken

explanation.surface: A brewery's line of beers, with a European one sent abroad in place of the leading Pilsner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head of' gives P, the first letter of Pilsner, and 'exported for' sends the E out of ALES with P in its place. 'Range' looks like a product line, but it is mountains.
explanation.definitionFit: The Alps are a mountain range spanning several countries of central Europe.

clue.text: Slice of Roquefort goes with fab black bitter

parts.note: ace and fab are both slang for excellent

indicators.note: a slice is a small piece taken off the end, so just one letter is kept

parts.note: the first letter of the cheese
B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A piece of French blue cheese pairs well with a great dark bitter beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bitter' looks like a dark beer to wash down the cheese, but it is the definition. The pieces are taken in a different order from the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Acerb is a rare synonym of acerbic, describing a sour, harsh or sharp taste or temper.

clue.text: A pair of Charlies pinching a half-French fellow?

indicators.note: to pinch something is to grip it from both sides, so one piece is held inside

parts.note: taken as written
Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet, and a pair gives two
taken as written
demi is the French prefix for half

explanation.surface: Two fools are stealing from a man who is half French.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half-French' reads as someone's ancestry, but means 'half' in French. The two Cs grip A and DEMI between them, after the opening A.
explanation.definitionFit: A fellow is a senior member of a college or university, so this is a scholar who teaches or researches.

clue.text: One linked to live broadcast around ancient region

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
to be is to exist, to live

indicators.note: to turn around is to face the other way, so this piece is read backwards

parts.note: to air a programme is to broadcast it

explanation.surface: A radio show transmitted live from somewhere in the ancient world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Live broadcast' reads as one phrase, but they are separate pieces; 'live' is the verb, rhyming with give.
explanation.definitionFit: Iberia was the classical name for the peninsula now holding Spain and Portugal, a region of antiquity.

clue.text: Don Lycra trousers and nothing more besides

indicators.note: as a verb, to trouser is to pocket something, so the letters are tucked inside the words

parts.note: the letters sit across the two words

explanation.surface: Someone puts on Lycra leggings and wears nothing else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trousers' looks like clothing that 'Don' puts on, but it is a verb meaning pockets, holding the answer inside the words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Only means merely, solely, with nothing added, as in 'only one', so nothing further is included.

clue.text: Spooner's purchased a comic in a drink store

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner swapped the first sounds of words, so the opening sounds of the two parts change places

parts.note: purchased a is bought a, said aloud like the first half of the phrase
a wag is a joker, a comic person

explanation.surface: Someone bought a comedian, odd in a shop selling drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spooner's' works on the phrase bought a wag; swapping its opening B and W sounds gives the answer. A store here is something that holds a supply, not a shop.
explanation.definitionFit: A water bag is a container of skin or canvas for carrying water, so it stores drink.
